metadata.note: Schematic hand-sketched polygons. Not surveyed borders. Not smoothed. Persia omitted.

properties.name: Assyria — Levant holdings and Mesopotamian heartland (schematic)
properties.claim: Around the fall of Samaria, Assyria is the power holding the northern Levant and the Assyrian heartland on the Tigris. This blob is that corridor: Nineveh, Kalhu (Nimrud), Dur-Sharrukin, and Assur, west through Carchemish and Sam'al into Syria, Phoenicia, and the old northern kingdom. It is a sketch of control, not a provincial map.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Babylon is left out on purpose. Around 722 Merodach-baladan is holding Babylon against Assyria, so a solid Assyrian fill there would be a ghost empire. Egypt, Urartu, and Elam are outside the box. The line stops at the Zagros foothills and the upper Tigris; it does not trace mountain frontiers. Philistine Ashdod is outside this polygon. Coastal Philistia is not drawn as an Assyrian province in 722. Where this fill barely overlaps the Judah polygon, that sliver is the fuzzy Israel/Judah border near Bethel, not two empires sharing a capital. Damascus has been in the Assyrian orbit since Tiglath-pileser III took it (732). There is no Damascus dig pin on the map; the city is inside the polygon only as geography.
sources: Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East c. 3000–330 BC (London: Routledge, 1995) — Assyrian, Babylonian, and Median extents after the fall of Nineveh.
Ephraim Stern, Archaeology of the Land of the Bible, Vol. II: The Assyrian, Babylonian, and Persian Periods (New York: Doubleday, 2001) — Levant under the empires.
Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings (Anchor Bible; New York: Doubleday, 1988) — 722, 701, and 586 campaigns.
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World (Jerusalem: Carta, 2006) — biblical-period historical geography and atlas maps.
Yohanan Aharoni and Michael Avi-Yonah, The Macmillan Bible Atlas, rev. ed. (New York: Macmillan, 1977) — period maps used as a sketch tradition, not as surveyed borders.

properties.name: Judah — surviving highland kingdom (schematic vassal, not annexed)
properties.claim: When Samaria falls, Judah is still a kingdom in the southern highlands and the Shephelah. It is already in Assyria's orbit (Ahaz had asked Assyria for help), but it is not turned into an Assyrian province. Paint this on top of any border sliver.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Do not treat the outline as the tribal allotment of Judah. Tribal maps are a later pack. Ashdod stays outside (Philistine). Lachish, Hebron, Arad, and Jerusalem (City of David) stay inside. Gezer is on the western edge and may be a border town — the line is not that precise. Jericho is included as a rift-valley edge of the southern kingdom, not as a claim that the border was surveyed to the Jordan. Which king is on the throne in the exact year 722 (Ahaz, or a Hezekiah co-regency) is debated. The polygon does not depend on that argument. This is a vassal kingdom inside an imperial world, not a second empire.
sources: Yohanan Aharoni, The Land of the Bible: A Historical Geography, 2nd ed. (Philadelphia: Westminster, 1979) — territorial history of Israel and Judah.
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World (Jerusalem: Carta, 2006) — biblical-period historical geography and atlas maps.

properties.name: Former Israel — absorbed outline (not a living kingdom)
properties.claim: The northern kingdom ends when Samaria falls. This outline is only a memory of where that kingdom sat (hill country, Jezreel, Galilee). It is not a state you can toggle as still alive. Draw it dashed, with no fill, so it does not look like a second country under Assyria.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Label it 'former Israel — absorbed,' or leave it off if a dashed outline is too easy to misread as a living border. Tyre and Sidon are outside on purpose. They were Phoenician cities, not Israelite territory. The old kingdom's exact tribes and Transjordan districts are not drawn. This is the core a map user already has pins for. People from these towns were deported and other peoples were settled in (2 Kings 17). The outline does not show those movements.

properties.name: Assyria — heartland plus 701 campaign zone in Judah's west (schematic)
properties.claim: In Sennacherib's campaign year Assyria still holds the same heartland and the Levant, and the army is in Judah's western lowlands. The fill comes south through the Shephelah and the Philistine coast so Lachish and Ashdod sit in the campaign zone. Jerusalem also falls inside this large orbit polygon. That does not mean Jerusalem was annexed — paint reduced Judah on top.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Babylon is still omitted. Sennacherib spends these years fighting there; it is a war zone, not a settled province to color in. The Assyrian text says many Judahite cities were taken and Hezekiah was shut up in Jerusalem. Those cities are not dotted. Lachish is the one city called out because the map already has the pin and the palace reliefs. Overlap with the reduced-Judah polygon means 'vassal pocket inside the imperial orbit,' not double rule of the same kind. Draw Judah above this fill. Egypt is not invaded in this sketch. The south edge stops at the Philistine coast.
sources: Daniel David Luckenbill, The Annals of Sennacherib (OIP 2; Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1924) — Sennacherib's claim to have taken Judahite cities and confined Hezekiah to Jerusalem. Paraphrased; the city list is not plotted.

properties.name: Judah — highland remnant after Sennacherib (schematic)
properties.claim: After the 701 campaign Hezekiah still holds Jerusalem and the highland core. This small polygon is that leftover kingdom. It is a cartoon of 'what was left,' not a plot of the 46 cities named in Sennacherib's annals.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Solidity is weak because the edges are a guess. The fact that Jerusalem was not taken, and that the western lowlands were overrun, is the part that is solid. Lachish, Gezer, Arad, and Ashdod are outside this polygon on purpose. Lachish was besieged and taken. Do not 'fix' the polygon to include it. Draw this on top of the Assyria fill. Where they overlap, Judah is the vassal pocket. The Bible says the Assyrian army left and Jerusalem stood (2 Kings 19). The Assyrian annals stress the siege and the tribute. Both can be true; the polygon is not a winner's trophy.
sources: Daniel David Luckenbill, The Annals of Sennacherib (OIP 2; Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1924) — Sennacherib's claim to have taken Judahite cities and confined Hezekiah to Jerusalem. Paraphrased; the city list is not plotted.

properties.name: Neo-Babylonian empire — Babylon heartland and the Levant (schematic)
properties.claim: By the fall of Jerusalem, the Neo-Babylonian empire holds Babylon and the south Mesopotamian heartland, the Euphrates route up to Carchemish, and the Levant that used to be Assyria's west. Judah is inside this fill because the kingdom has been destroyed and the land is Babylon's.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. The old Assyrian triangle is not colored Babylonian. Nineveh, Nimrud, Khorsabad, and Assur sit outside. After 612 that northland is mostly Median. Media is not one of the locked polities, so it is absent instead of invented. Susa and Ecbatana are outside. Elam and the Iranian plateau are not this empire's drawn core. Egypt is the neighbor across the Sinai edge, not inside the polygon. Nebuchadnezzar fought Egypt; he did not swallow it. Carchemish (605) is the northern Syrian edge this sketch is willing to claim. Zincirli / Sam'al is left outside as too far into the mountains. A smaller 'former Judah' outline sits on top. It is a label, not a surviving kingdom.
sources: Amélie Kuhrt, The Ancient Near East c. 3000–330 BC (London: Routledge, 1995) — Assyrian, Babylonian, and Median extents after the fall of Nineveh.

properties.name: Former Judah — destroyed kingdom, now Babylonian (outline only)
properties.claim: Judah is not an independent kingdom in 586. This outline marks the land that had been the kingdom so a user can still see it under the Babylonian fill. Label: 'former Judah, now Babylonian.' No fill.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Gedaliah governs a remnant from Mizpah for Babylon (2 Kings 25). That is an administration, not a restored kingdom, and Mizpah is not given a new pin. Ashdod stays outside the outline. It was not a Judahite royal city. Do not read the outline as the 586 siege wall or as the tribal border.
sources: Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings (Anchor Bible; New York: Doubleday, 1988) — 722, 701, and 586 campaigns.

properties.name: Roman Syria — provincial core (Antioch, Phoenician coast, Damascus)
properties.claim: The nearer Roman frame for Jesus' day is the province of Syria, governed from Antioch. This sketch is that core: Antioch, the coast through Sidon and Tyre, and Damascus. It is not a polygon of the Mediterranean, and it is not painted over Judea or Galilee.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Decapolis cities (HIPP-01 Hippos is the pin) belong to this Syrian orbit but do not get their own polygon. One blob would swallow Galilee. Mention them in the panel, do not re-pin. The south edge stops above Philip's box and above Galilee. A hairline gap is better than a fake shared border. The province of Syria legally reached farther than this cartoon. The cartoon is the part that explains the digs. Assyria, Babylon, and Persia are not drawn at this date. They are gone.
sources: Emil Schürer, The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ, rev. Geza Vermes and Fergus Millar, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1973) — prefecture of Judea and the Herodian tetrarchies.
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World (Jerusalem: Carta, 2006) — biblical-period historical geography and atlas maps.
Yohanan Aharoni and Michael Avi-Yonah, The Macmillan Bible Atlas, rev. ed. (New York: Macmillan, 1977) — period maps used as a sketch tradition, not as surveyed borders.

properties.name: Roman Judea — prefecture of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea (schematic)
properties.claim: In Jesus' adult years Judea is not a kingdom. A Roman prefect (Pontius Pilate, about 26–36 CE) governs Judea, Samaria, and Idumea from Caesarea. This polygon is that prefecture: Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Hebron, Jericho, Samaria, Joppa, and Caesarea. It is not a map of the whole Roman Empire.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Galilee is a different feature (Herod Antipas). Do not merge them. Megiddo and the Jezreel valley are left in the gap between this polygon and Galilee. Assigning that valley to either side would fake a border we do not have. Gaza and the Nabatean south are not carefully traced. The south edge is Idumea in cartoon form. Rome the city is the ROME-01 / ROME-02 / ROME-03 pins. Do not stretch this polygon to Italy. Herod the Great's united kingdom is already over (he dies in 4 BCE). This is the split map.
sources: Emil Schürer, The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ, rev. Geza Vermes and Fergus Millar, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1973) — prefecture of Judea and the Herodian tetrarchies.
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World (Jerusalem: Carta, 2006) — biblical-period historical geography and atlas maps.

properties.name: Herod Antipas — Galilee (schematic tetrarchy)
properties.claim: Herod Antipas is tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, not a Roman prefect and not a king of the Jews. This piece is only Galilee: Nazareth, Sepphoris, and Capernaum on the lake. Perea is a second polygon because one ring cannot jump the Jordan.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Client ruler under Rome, not an independent empire. Luke 3:1 names him beside Pilate on purpose. Hippos (HIPP-01) is a Decapolis city east of the lake and stays outside. Do not pull the polygon across the lake to grab it. Tyre and Sidon are in the Syria feature, not Galilee. Caesarea Philippi / Banias is Philip's tetrarchy, not Antipas. Megiddo is left in the gap south of this polygon.
sources: Emil Schürer, The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ, rev. Geza Vermes and Fergus Millar, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1973) — prefecture of Judea and the Herodian tetrarchies.
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World (Jerusalem: Carta, 2006) — biblical-period historical geography and atlas maps.

properties.name: Herod Antipas — Perea, east of the Jordan (schematic)
properties.claim: Perea is the other half of Antipas's tetrarchy: a strip east of the Jordan, roughly from opposite Jericho up toward the Decapolis edge. No existing dig pin sits in the strip, and none is invented.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Solidity is weak. Ancient writers agree Antipas held Perea; they do not agree on a fence line. Machaerus is the famous fortress of this region and is not a pin on this map. Do not add one from this pack. Philadelphia (Amman) and Hippos are Decapolis and stay outside. Jericho is west of the river and stays in the Judea polygon.
sources: Emil Schürer, The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ, rev. Geza Vermes and Fergus Millar, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1973) — prefecture of Judea and the Herodian tetrarchies.
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World (Jerusalem: Carta, 2006) — biblical-period historical geography and atlas maps.

properties.name: Philip — Gaulanitis and Paneas (schematic tetrarchy)
properties.claim: Luke 3:1 also names Philip as tetrarch of Iturea and Trachonitis. At about 30 CE he is still ruling (he dies in 34). This box is only the part we can place without swallowing Galilee or Damascus: the Golan / Banias block, including Dan and Caesarea Philippi.
properties.caveats: Approximate political sketch, not a surveyed boundary. The line shows who roughly controlled the region, not a GPS border. Expect tens of kilometers of error. Do not zoom in and read a vertex as a real frontier post. Iturea and Trachonitis extend farther north and east than this box. Those edges are fuzzy, so they are not drawn. The box will look too small if you treat it as Philip's whole title. Solidity is weak on the line, mixed-to-strong on the fact that Banias is Philip's city. Not Antipas, not the Decapolis, not the prefecture of Judea. Lysanias of Abilene is named in the same verse and is not drawn. Abilene is a small district around the Anti-Lebanon with no pin and no clean polygon here.
sources: Emil Schürer, The History of the Jewish People in the Age of Jesus Christ, rev. Geza Vermes and Fergus Millar, vol. 1 (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1973) — prefecture of Judea and the Herodian tetrarchies.
Anson F. Rainey and R. Steven Notley, The Sacred Bridge: Carta's Atlas of the Biblical World (Jerusalem: Carta, 2006) — biblical-period historical geography and atlas maps.
